item.title: Four Ways to Avoid the AI Writing Slop-a-Thon
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Four Ways to Avoid the AI Writing Slop-a-Thon

Many writers turn to AI because they never learned how writing works.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Writers use AI because they don't understand they can control how readers respond to their writing.
  • Research on priming reveals that titles and subheadings strongly influence readers' understandings of content.
  • Studies demonstrate that primary and recency effects determine how readers recall content.
  • In clinical studies, transitions and sequences that tie sentences together improve reading speeds.

Last week, Nature reported that 90% of published biomedicine papers used some form of AI assistance. And that statistic covers manuscripts that editors thought worthy of publication, not the scores of AI-generated rejects editors discarded.

Unfortunately, if you own a computer, smartphone, or any digital device, you’re all too familiar with AI slop. Generic content, clickbait headlines, and weirdly wordy content that turns some social media posts into miniature versions of War and Peace—minus content you actually want to read.

Sure, writing is onerous and time-consuming, compared to typing three sentences into Claude and pasting the result.

However, many writers turn to AI because they fear writing. For virtually all writers, despite years of high school and college writing courses, writing remains a black box. Experts call a system a black box when we know the inputs (writing) and outputs (our readers’ reactions) but lack knowledge of what takes place inside the system. Most writers lack any sense of how writing works. In addition, many of us have ample and unfortunate experience in completing what we imagined was a strong assignment, article, or manuscript, only to have some authority tear our sentences to shreds.

Source: Mikhail Nilov, Pexels

1. Writing is not a black box

Contrary to popular belief, writing anxiety barely affects the quality of writing. However, if you feel writing is a game where you know few of the rules, AI comes across as a good bet in what otherwise seems like a crapshoot.

Ironically, researchers in psycholinguistics decades ago identified useful insights into how writing works, which few writing teachers include in their courses. Nevertheless, from that research, we can draw guidelines that make writing easier, faster, and understandable.

2. Use titles and subheadings to powerfully prime readers’ impressions of content.

In fact, subheadings shape our understanding of content so strongly that readers recall content following subheadings as consistent with them—even when it is inconsistent. At the same time, these subheadings enable writers to create the central points of any document quickly and relatively painlessly. This step also eliminates some of the terror of the blank page that afflicts so many writers. Furthermore, these subheadings enable writers to identify the through-line in their thinking, and they can experience their documents from their readers’ perspective.

article continues after advertisement

3. Place important information at beginnings and endings.

We recall information differently, depending on where we encounter it. Readers typically show stronger recall of content in the beginnings and endings of lists, sentences, and paragraphs. At the same time, readers typically spend more time reading the first few sentences in paragraphs than they do the rest of the content, anticipating those early sentences will provide a framework for understanding the content that follows them. On the other hand, if you want readers to forget content you must disclose, drop it into a dead zone: the middles of sentences in the middles of paragraphs.

4. Tie sentences together with sequences and transitions.

Use these positions at the beginnings and endings of sentences to tie them together. Sentences in English rely on sentence structure, rather than content, to determine their beginnings and endings. The result: Sentences that resemble islands of meaning, separated by gaps that rely on readers to determine the connections between them. Unsurprisingly, these gaps between sentences decrease reading speeds as writers must infer connections.

However, writers can easily connect sentences in two ways. 1) They can use transitions at the beginning of one sentence to signal whether the sentence continues, causes, revises, or illustrates the content from the preceding sentence. 2) Writers can connect content from the end of one sentence to the beginning of the next by using common wording or references to that content.

These principles enable writers to control readers’ reactions to their writing by anticipating how our reading brains respond to words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents.

Source: Muhammad-Taha Ibrahim, Pexels

item.title: Does Having a Crush Mean Your Relationship Is in Trouble?
item.description:
Relationships

Does Having a Crush Mean Your Relationship Is in Trouble?

New research suggests attraction outside commitment is often benign.

Posted August 27, 2026

Key points
  • A fleeting crush doesn’t necessarily mean your relationship is in trouble. Commitment matters most.
  • Risk increases when dissatisfaction leads you to seek, fantasize about, or pursue romantic alternatives.
  • Protect your relationship by reinvesting in connection, setting boundaries, and communicating openly.
Source: Edmond Dantès/Pexels

After over 12 years of facilitating couples therapy with hundreds of couples, my advice for a healthy monogamous relationship is to stay romantically focused on your partner. Especially in Los Angeles or other major metropolitan areas where there are lots of attractive people who can become a distraction or source of fantasy with destructive consequences. However, attraction to someone outside of your relationship is not necessarily fatal to a long love.

I first heard this contrary point as a young Marine stationed in Japan, walking with a supervisor across our base who exchanged a smile with a gorgeous older woman passing by us. I was 18 and my boss was in his 40s and married. He said something to me that day that has stuck with me, “Matos, it doesn’t matter where you get your appetite, as long as you eat at home.”

Surprising recent research suggests that the salty Marine was partially right. If you’ve been in a committed relationship and have been attracted to other people or even had a fleeting crush, it doesn’t immediately equate to significant trouble for your relationship (O’Sullivan, Belu, & Tramonte, 2025).

I’ve worked with many clients, mostly men, on discerning their commitment to their romantic relationships. Often this discernment kicks off after they experience romantic or sexual attraction to women outside of their committed relationships. The phenomenon is not limited to men and there's growing evidence that it is a common experience with upwards of 70% of adults in monogamous relationships reporting attraction to someone other than their partner (Mullinax et al, 2016).

Attraction may occur with in-person interactions with known others (i.e. workplace professional relationships) but it can also happen on social media platforms with unknown others and/or parasocial relationships.

There are several levels of interpretation of connections with attractive extra-relational persons that determine an increasing risk of relationship deterioration. To be attracted to someone else is one thing, to view someone else as a potential alternative to your partner is a more precarious situation. Considering romantic alternatives is largely a function of relationship satisfaction (Abbasi & Alghamdi, 2018).

Examples of Situational Risk in Attraction Outside the Relationship

Here are several hypotheticals with increasing risk to your committed relationship:

  1. Low Risk: You’re satisfied in your current relationship and are infrequently interacting with others who you find sexually attractive, in-person or online.
  2. Moderate Risk: You’re somewhat dissatisfied in your current romance and find yourself actively seeking interactions in-person or on social media with attractive others.
  3. High Risk: You’re dissatisfied in your marriage or long-term relationship and you have frequent, consistent contact with sexually attractive colleagues or community members.
article continues after advertisement

I’ve written often on this page about the fundamental necessity for trust and commitment in long-term relationships. Commitment is a function of focus and future-orientation on the longevity of your monogamous connection to your partner. It is about engaging in behaviors that fortify your relationship, to include couples therapy when romantic or sexual dissatisfaction creeps up in a long-term love. Trust is reinforced by consistently making good decisions that level up your fondness and admiration for one another, emotional connection, and transparent communication. In the absence of significant dissatisfaction and high levels of commitment, fleeting crushes can be fairly benign.

Strategies to Handle Developing Feelings for Someone Else

If you’ve found yourself in a sticky situation where you’re developing an intimate, emotional connection with someone you see frequently, here’s a few suggestions:

  1. Focus on your marriage or long-term relationship. Where there is negative sentiment override (emotional exhaustion from conflict), changes in the quality of your sexual lives, and dissatisfaction—address it now. Don’t wait. Make repair and emotional attunement a priority. Reinvest and strengthen your attachment. Seek couples therapy with a well-trained and experienced couples psychologist.
  2. Don’t entertain fantasies if you’re dissatisfied in your relationship. Turn toward your partner and bid for romantic and sexual connection. The dopaminergic response from initially fantasizing about the extra-relational person or worse, masturbating thinking about them, will only reinforce the idea of them as a viable alternative to your partner. Use cognitive-behavioral strategies of distraction, thought stopping, and treating fantasies as cognitive distortions by challenging them: this isn’t an option, this isn’t helpful, I’m committed to my partner, etc.
  3. Set clear boundaries for yourself and limit interactions. Commit to professional interactions free of innuendo or anything resembling flirting. Do not disclose or discuss challenges in your romantic relationship with this person. Do not seek to spend more time with them than is absolutely necessary. Do not nurture emotional intimacy.

The good news is that healthy, long-term love can withstand the trials of modern life and prevail in the midst of a thousand temptations over decades. Being amongst attractive people and even the occasional fleeting crush has nothing on a fierce committed, monogamous relationship. And the growing challenges of potential emotional infidelity on social media or in the workplace can be successfully neutralized with a focus on nurturing a satisfying love with novelty and open, gentle communication.
